inss_desc_assoc.titulo: Association membership dues deducted from INSS benefits
inss_desc_assoc.serie_codigo: Relatório de Avaliação nº 1675291 (set/2024, anos de 2016 a 2023) e Relatório de Avaliação nº 1745585 (dez/2024, valor realizado de 2024)
inss_desc_assoc.criterio: Total amount deducted each year from the retirement and survivor benefits paid by the INSS as membership dues for associations, unions and pensioners' organizations, through the Technical Cooperation Agreements signed with the institute. It is the TOTAL deducted: within these figures the CGU does not separate the share authorized by the beneficiary from the unauthorized share, and it publishes no monetary estimate of the irregular portion. Reading this series as 'the value of the fraud' is an error — it measures how much left the benefits, not how much left them improperly. The figures come from the CGU's own extraction of the INSS Maciça database, covering January 2016 to May 2024, and the CGU states that they are underestimated by around 20%, because the shared database carries only the first ten line items of each benefit and 9.6 million of the 40.1 million benefits have more than ten. The series is therefore a floor, not a total. There is no official figure before 2016 — not because the deduction did not exist (it has been authorised since the original wording of Law 8.213/1991, art. 115, V), but because the payroll shared by the INSS only has history from January 2016. There is no 2025 total because the deductions were suspended in April of that year; the only month released is January 2025, at R$257.1 million.

fonte.nome: CGU — Relatório de Avaliação nº 1675291, sobre descontos de mensalidades associativas em benefícios do INSS

notas.nota: The 2024 figure (R$2.8 billion) is the REALIZED amount, established in CGU Report No. 1745585, completed in December 2024, and was released rounded — the exact number, with decimal places, was not found in any source accessible in this collection. It supersedes the projection of R$2,637.2 million published months earlier in Report No. 1675291, which extrapolated May 2024 as constant for the rest of the year. The two numbers circulate in the press as though they were the same figure; they are not. Source for the realized figure: https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/geral/noticia/2025-05/cgu-recomendou-suspensao-de-descontos-em-folha-de-aposentados

The entire series is underestimated by roughly 20% by the CGU's own declaration: the database shared by the INSS is limited to the first ten line items of each benefit, and 23.9% of benefits have more than ten line items. The figures are a floor, not a total.

The 'R$6.3 billion' attributed to the Federal Police investigation corresponds exactly to the sum of this series between 2019 and 2024 (R$6,295.0 million, using the 2024 projection rather than the realized figure). It is not an independent estimate of misappropriation: it is the total deducted in the period. The Federal Police itself uses the phrase 'estimated amount' charged, not amount misappropriated.
The series ends in 2024 because the deductions were suspended by the INSS in April 2025, after Operation No Deduction. No annual total for 2025 has been published.

The series starting in 2016 does not mean the deduction began there. Deducting an association's membership fee straight from the benefit is in the original text of Law 8.213 of 24 July 1991 (art. 115, item V) — twenty-five years older than the first bar on this chart. What begins in 2016 is the database: the payroll the INSS shared with the CGU only has history from January of that year. Reading the chart as 'the scheme began in 2016' mistakes the limit of the extraction for the beginning of the fact. Source for the law: https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/leis/l8213compilado.htm

The mechanism has been abolished. Law 15.327 of 6 January 2026 repealed item V of art. 115 of Law 8.213/1991 and inserted a provision barring any deduction of association membership fees from an INSS benefit. The chart therefore describes a mechanism that existed from 1991 to 2026. Source: https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2023-2026/2026/lei/l15327.htm

pontos.obs: realized figure released rounded (R$2.8 billion), from CGU Report No. 1745585; the earlier projection, from Report No. 1675291, was R$2,637.2 million

inss_ressarcimento.titulo: Refunds of deductions to beneficiaries — cumulative amount
inss_ressarcimento.serie_codigo: Balanços do INSS sobre a devolução de descontos associativos e depoimento do presidente do INSS à CPMI
inss_ressarcimento.criterio: Cumulative amount already refunded by the INSS to beneficiaries who challenged membership-dues deductions, measured on the date indicated at each point. It is a measure of accumulated STOCK, not an annual figure: each point contains the previous ones. The refunds cover deductions made between March 2020 and March 2025, and the final deadline to file a challenge closed on 20 March 2026. Only points with a date and value released by the INSS or stated by the institute's president are included here; figures from aggregators with no attribution to an official source were discarded.

fonte.nome: INSS — balanço da devolução de descontos associativos, 26/12/2025

notas.nota: The December 2025 point is the only one with an exact value published by the INSS: R$2,820,799,182.93, covering 4,137,951 payments generated. The April 2026 point is rounded. Between the two there is an intermediate measurement not shown on the chart, so as not to overlay two near-identical points: on 5 February 2026 the president of the INSS told the joint congressional inquiry that around R$2.9 billion had been refunded to 4.2 million beneficiaries.

The universe of challenges is larger than that of refunds: more than 6.3 million applications were filed by beneficiaries questioning deductions, and around 6.2 million of them stated they had not authorized the deduction (INSS balance of 26/12/2025).

Official balances after April 2026 could not be confirmed in this collection: the INSS balance pages on gov.br returned restricted content and Agência Brasil is off the air under electoral-law restrictions. Figures for July and August 2026 circulating on aggregator sites were not included, for lack of attribution to an official source.

25/04/2026 — 'more than R$3 billion' to around 4.4 million insured people, released to the press with attribution to the INSS; figure rounded down

inss_teto.unidade: R$ (at current prices of each year)
inss_teto.orgao: Ministério da Previdência Social / Ministério da Fazenda — portarias interministeriais de reajuste
inss_teto.serie_codigo: Portarias interministeriais MPS/MF (e, antes de 2019, MPAS, MPS e ME) que fixam a tabela de contribuição
inss_teto.criterio: The highest contribution salary on which the social-security deduction falls for employees, domestic workers and casual workers — that is, the limit above which salary generates no contribution and does not count towards calculating the benefit. Each year's point is the ceiling IN FORCE AT THE END OF THAT YEAR, because the adjustment usually happens mid-year and a single year can have two ceilings. Nominal values, not adjusted for inflation: the rise of the line reflects annual adjustments and accumulated inflation, not a real increase in contribution.

fonte.nome: Portaria Interministerial MPS/MF nº 13, de 9 de janeiro de 2026 (tabela vigente) e tabela histórica de contribuição do INSS

notas.nota: The official INSS table available on gov.br covers only recent years. The values from 1998 to 2017 were obtained from compilations of contribution tables maintained by accounting-services providers, cross-checked against each other; the original ministerial orders from that period are not held in any accessible public repository. These are secondary sources, and that is declared here rather than omitted.
The 1998 point (R$1,200.00) was in force only from 16 to 31 December of that year; for the rest of 1998 the ceiling was R$1,031.87 and then R$1,081.50.
The jump from 2003 to 2004 is not an ordinary adjustment: the ceiling was set at R$2,400.00 by Constitutional Amendment 41/2003 and then adjusted to R$2,508.72 in May 2004.
Two compilations disagree on the 2010 ceiling: R$3,416.54 and R$3,416.24. The difference is 30 cents and it could not be settled against a primary source in this collection.

From 1 March 2020, by effect of Constitutional Amendment 103/2019, the deduction ceased to be a single rate on the whole salary and became progressive by bracket, as in income tax. The nominal rate of the top bracket (14%) is therefore not what is paid on the entire salary: someone earning the ceiling in 2026 has R$988.09 deducted, equivalent to 11.66% effective.

ibovespa.orgao: B3 (Brasil, Bolsa, Balcão) — e, para os anos recentes, imprensa financeira com atribuição à B3
ibovespa.serie_codigo: Resumo de Variação Anual do Ibovespa (tabela oficial da B3, 1968-2020) e divulgações de fechamento anual (2021 em diante)
ibovespa.criterio: Percentage change of the Bovespa Index over the year, measured from the close of the year's last trading session against the close of the previous year's last session, in reais. Two features of the index change how it reads and are usually overlooked. The first: the Ibovespa has been a TOTAL RETURN index since its origin — dividends, interest on equity and subscription rights are reinvested in the theoretical portfolio. That makes it incomparable with pure price indices in the form they are normally published, such as the S&P 500; the correct comparison would be against that index's total-return version. The second: the values are nominal, with no inflation adjustment — in years of high inflation, a positive change can still mean a loss of purchasing power. No official inflation-adjusted Ibovespa series is published by any public source, and this site does not compute its own.

fonte.nome: B3 — Resumo de Variação Anual do Ibovespa

notas.nota: The years 1998 to 2020 come from B3's official table, to two decimal places. From 2021 on the official table is not accessible: B3's legacy page ends in 2020 and the new one is generated by JavaScript, which the tools used in this collection do not read. The years 2021 to 2026 come from financial press reporting that attributes the figure to the market close — reinforced by B3 itself for 2025, which issued an institutional note confirming a rise of around 34%.

A methodology break without a series break. In 2014 the Ibovespa changed its weighting criterion: out went the Tradability Index and in came free-float market value, with a 20% cap per company and the exclusion of penny stocks — a change prompted by the OGX case. The transition was made in two stages, with mixed weighting from January to April 2014. B3 did NOT recalculate the published series, so the percentages here are those actually recorded at the time; what changes from 2014 on is the rule for composing the index, not the level of the series. A simulated retroactive series covering 34 quarters was released separately by BM&FBovespa, for study only: it does not replace the official one.

1999 is the best year in the series (+151.93%) and coincides with the sharp devaluation of the real and the adoption of a floating exchange rate and inflation targeting. 2008 is the worst (-41.22%), in the subprime crisis. Neither is the work of a government decision: the first follows a change of exchange-rate regime amid capital flight, the second is a global shock.
The 2026 point is partial: it measures from the close of 2025 through 11 September 2026 and changes with every trading session. It is not comparable with the closed years.

For 2025 sources disagree: 33.95% (InfoMoney and Forbes) and 34.10% (StatusInvest); B3 itself rounded to 34% in a note. We adopt 33.95% because the source publishing it reproduces the official figures for known years to the hundredth.

ministerios.titulo: Posts with ministerial rank in the federal executive
ministerios.orgao: Presidência da República — leis orgânicas da Esplanada dos Ministérios
ministerios.criterio: Number of posts holding the rank or prerogatives of Minister of State on 31 December of each year, counted from the legal text in force on that date. It includes the heads of the ministries proper and the Presidency bodies whose chiefs the law declares Ministers of State — today the Chief of Staff's Office, the Secretariat-General, the Secretariat of Institutional Relations, the Secretariat of Social Communication, the Institutional Security Cabinet and the Solicitor General's Office. The Comptroller General is counted because the current law lists it inside the list of ministries itself. The Governor of the central bank counts from 22/12/2004, when Law 11,036 turned the post into a Minister of State, until 23/02/2021, when Complementary Law 179 removed that status; before and after, it does not count. Counting 'ministries' is slippery precisely because each source adds up a different set: that is why the criterion is written out here, and why the numbers in this chart differ from compilations that do not state theirs.

fonte.nome: Lei 14.600/2023 (texto compilado) e demais leis orgânicas da Esplanada, no portal da Casa Civil

notas.nota: Between 2003 and 2009 the article listing the Ministers of State was NOT exhaustive: Provisional Measure 103/2003 created, in a separate article, four Special Secretaries with 'prerogatives, guarantees, advantages and rights equivalent to those of a Minister of State' — Aquaculture and Fisheries, Policies for Women, Human Rights, and the Economic and Social Development Council — plus an Extraordinary Minister for Food Security. None of them appeared on the list. There are therefore, for those years, two rigorous counts of the same legal criterion, differing by as much as four. This series uses the broader count, which includes every post with ministerial rank: it is the only one that coincides with the strict count from 2010 onward and therefore the only one that produces a comparable line across the whole period. Under the strict count, the values from 2003 to 2009 would be 29, 31, 30, 30, 31, 33 and 34.

The years 1999, 2000 and 2001 are not in the series. The cabinet was reorganized in that period by provisional measures reissued month after month, until they were frozen by Constitutional Amendment 32/2001; establishing who held ministerial rank on 31 December of each of those years would require identifying which reissue was in force on that exact date, which was not possible with the accessible sources. The chart prefers a declared gap to an estimated number.

For 2006 and 2012 no act altering the structure was found, and the value comes from continuity between the neighboring years, not from a direct reading of the law. The absence of a located act is not proof that no act existed: these two are the weakest points in the series.

2015 has two real values. Until 1 October there were 39 — the record for the whole series. Provisional Measure 696, of 02/10/2015, abolished eight portfolios and cut the total to 31, which is the 31 December value used here. The same applies to 2024: the structure reached 39 between 15 May and 9 September, with the Extraordinary Secretariat for Support to the Reconstruction of Rio Grande do Sul, and returned to 38 when the provisional measure lapsed.

2016 is the smallest top tier in the series, at 26, and the reason is little known: besides abolishing portfolios, Law 13,341/2016 repealed three items from the list of Ministers of State, and the Secretariat-General of the Presidency was left without ministerial rank until February 2017. Note that 2019 has fewer MINISTRIES than 2016 but more posts holding ministerial rank.

On 1 January 2023 there were 37, under Provisional Measure 1,154; in August the Ministry of Entrepreneurship raised it to 38, which is the end-of-year value and remains in force. Today there are 38, not 39: the 39 in circulation usually comes from adding the Governor of the central bank, who lost ministerial rank in February 2021, or from carrying into the present the peak of May to September 2024.

The series was assembled from three direct readings of the legal text — Law 11,497/2007, Law 12,314/2010 and Provisional Measure 696/2015 restate the entire list of Ministers of State and work as complete snapshots — and, between them, from adding up dated acts of creation and abolition. The three snapshots agree with what the sum of acts predicted, with nothing left over.

arrecadacao_real.serie_codigo: Análise Mensal da Arrecadação das Receitas Federais — Tabela III, SUBTOTAL [C], deflacionada pelo IPCA/IBGE
arrecadacao_real.criterio: Federal Revenue Service of Brazil (RFB): the sum of revenue administered by the RFB and social-security contributions — in Table I of the RFB reports, the line SUBTOTAL [C]. This aggregate is NOT the figure the RFB announces as a headline each January: the headline is TOTAL GERAL [E], which also adds revenue administered by other bodies (dividends, royalties, concessions) and is about R$ 124 billion larger in 2025. SUBTOTAL [C] is used here because it is the aggregate that corresponds to taxes and contributions, and because it is the only one consistently available across the whole series since 1995. Federal revenue only: state taxes (ICMS, vehicle tax) and municipal taxes (service tax, property tax) are not included. The RFB's current-price figures were converted to December 2025 reais using the IBGE's accumulated IPCA inflation index (December-to-December change in each year), a series this site already publishes. The calculation is this site's, not the RFB's — the RFB publishes its own deflated table, but with a base year that changes with every monthly report, which makes it unsuitable for a fixed series. Correcting by December IPCA is the usual convention; anyone who prefers the year's average IPCA will find slightly different figures in the high-inflation years.

fonte.nome: Receita Federal do Brasil — Análise Mensal da Arrecadação das Receitas Federais, anexo estatístico, Tabela III (série 1995-2026, a preços correntes)

notas.nota: The RFB table begins in 1995. This series begins in 1998 to match the window of the other charts in this collection.
Base date for the correction: December 2025. By construction, the real figure for 2025 equals the current-price figure for 2025.

mortes_grupo.titulo: Deaths in Brazil by broad cause group
mortes_grupo.orgao: Ministério da Saúde/SVSA/CGIAE — Sistema de Informações sobre Mortalidade (SIM), via TabNet/DATASUS
mortes_grupo.serie_codigo: SIM/DATASUS — óbitos por residência, por ano do óbito e capítulo da CID-10
mortes_grupo.criterio: Number of deaths occurring in the year, by the deceased's place of residence, classified by underlying cause of death under the chapter headings of the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10). The underlying cause is the disease or event that began the chain leading to death, not the one listed last on the certificate. Each death counts once, in one chapter only. “Other chapters” adds up the eight smaller chapters (blood and immunity, mental disorders, eye, ear, skin, musculoskeletal, pregnancy and childbirth, congenital malformations), so the selector is not filled with lines pinned to zero. The twelve groups add up to exactly the total, in every year. Extracted by this site on 15 September 2026 from TabNet: deaths by place of residence, Brazil, rows and columns as indicated, all years from 1996 to 2025 (the series published here starts in 1998, to match the window of the other charts). According to DATASUS's own note on the extraction date, the data are final through 2024 (extracted 02/12/2025) and preliminary for 2025 (extracted 28/07/2026); 2025 is therefore marked as preliminary and may rise in later consolidations. In this DATASUS tabulation, covid-19 deaths fall under chapter I, infectious and parasitic diseases: that is what explains chapter I jumping from 56,666 deaths in 2019 to 267,287 in 2020 and 486,667 in 2021, and falling back to 73,442 in 2023. There is no separate covid chapter in this grid.

fonte.nome: Ministério da Saúde — Sistema de Informações sobre Mortalidade (SIM), tabulado no TabNet/DATASUS

notas.nota: 2025 data are preliminary according to DATASUS; consolidation usually raises the figures.

mortes_causa.orgao: Ministério da Saúde/SVSA/CGIAE — Sistema de Informações sobre Mortalidade (SIM), via TabNet/DATASUS
mortes_causa.serie_codigo: SIM/DATASUS — óbitos por residência, por ano do óbito e causa (lista CID-BR-10)
categorias: Cancer of the trachea, bronchi and lungs
mortes_causa.criterio: Number of deaths occurring in the year, by place of residence, classified by underlying cause of death under the ICD-BR-10 list, the cause list the Ministry of Health uses to tabulate mortality in Brazil. The fifteen causes here do not add up to total deaths, and are not meant to: they are slices taken from within the ICD-10 chapters. “Ischaemic heart disease” and “cerebrovascular disease” are the two largest components of the circulatory-system chapter; “assaults” is the same concept as the homicides series in this collection. Dengue appears by the underlying cause recorded on the death certificate, which is a smaller and later figure than deaths confirmed by epidemiological surveillance (SINAN): for 2024, 5,233 here against roughly 6,000 in the SINAN tally. They are two different counts of the same phenomenon, not an error in either. For 2025 dengue has no value in the tabulation and so does not enter the line. Covid-19 is the sum of ICD-10 categories B34 and U07 — B34.2 was the code used in 2020, before the World Health Organization created U07, adopted from 2021. The line starts in 2020 because the disease did not exist before that; the 20 to 240 deaths a year that B34 recorded before 2020 are other viral illnesses and were left out. By underlying cause on the death certificate, the SIM system totals 723,624 covid-19 deaths between 2020 and 2025 — close to, but not identical with, the roughly 716,000 in the Ministry of Health's notification dashboard, which counts by another route. Extracted by this site on 15 September 2026 from TabNet: deaths by place of residence, Brazil, rows and columns as indicated, all years from 1996 to 2025 (the series published here starts in 1998, to match the window of the other charts). According to DATASUS's own note on the extraction date, the data are final through 2024 (extracted 02/12/2025) and preliminary for 2025 (extracted 28/07/2026); 2025 is therefore marked as preliminary and may rise in later consolidations.

Covid-19: the sum of B34 and U07 in the ICD-10. In 2020 the disease was coded as B34.2; the U07 code took effect in 2021.

estatais_fluxo.titulo: Entries to and exits from the federal state-company list
estatais_fluxo.unidade: number of companies in the year
estatais_fluxo.orgao: MGI/SEST — cadastro de empresas estatais federais
estatais_fluxo.serie_codigo: Empresas Estatais Federais — ativas (datas de criação) e inativas desde 1990 (datas de saída)
estatais_fluxo.criterio: Counted by this site from the two official registers the SEST publishes monthly: the list of active federal state-owned companies, with each one's creation date, and the list of companies inactive since 1990, with the date each stopped being a federal state company. The series starts in 1990 because that is where the inactive register starts — and it is also the year the National Denationalization Programme was created (Law 8,031/1990). An exit here is any way of leaving the list: sale of control, absorption by another company, liquidation, closure or transfer — the register records the date, not a standardized reason, so it is not possible to separate privatization from absorption using it. In 1990-1991 that distinction is decisive: Law 8,029/1990 closed or wound up companies such as Embrater, EBTU, Portobras and Embrafilme, and merged Cobal, Cibrazem and CFP into Conab — none of those exits is a privatization. Two limits of the register, which this chart does not hide. First: of the 411 companies on the inactive list, 139 have no exit date recorded — and 49 of them belong to the Telebrás system. That is why 1998, the year of the largest privatization in the country's history, shows only two exits here: the 12 holdings auctioned in July 1998 are on the inactive list with no date. The chart measures what the register dates, not everything that happened. Second: the entries column counts the companies created in each year THAT STILL EXIST today. A company created after 1990 and already wound up does not appear, so the older years are more understated than the recent ones. One row with an exit year of 2111, an obvious register error, was discarded.

fonte.nome: Ministério da Gestão e da Inovação em Serviços Públicos (MGI) — Secretaria de Coordenação e Governança das Empresas Estatais (SEST), cadastro de empresas estatais federais ativas e inativas

notas.nota: Of the 15 exits in 1991, four are PND auctions (Usiminas, Celma, Mafersa and Cosinor, between October and November); the rest are closures, liquidations and mergers under Law 8,029/1990 — including Cobal, Cibrazem and CFP, merged to form Conab.
Collor was removed from office on 2 October 1992. Under this site's rule, a full year is attributed to whoever held office on 31 December — so, to Itamar Franco.
The 12 holding companies of the Telebrás system, auctioned in July 1998 for R$ 22.057 billion, are on the inactive list with no exit date and therefore do not enter the 1998 bar.
The 26 exits of 2022 are mostly the Eletrobras cascade: the holding plus Furnas, Chesf, Eletronorte, CGT Eletrosul and Eletropar left in the same move.

estatais_quantas.serie_codigo: Boletim das Empresas Estatais Federais e Relatório Agregado (SEST); Raio-X das Empresas Estatais Estaduais (STN)
categorias: Federal — Perfil das Estatais, companies published
Federal — with subsidiaries, criteria up to 2018
estatais_quantas.criterio: Three different counts, because there is no single one. “Direct control” means the companies in which the federal government is itself the majority shareholder — Petrobras, Banco do Brasil, Caixa, the post office, Embrapa and others. “With subsidiaries” adds the companies they control, at several levels, including those based abroad. “State-level” is the Treasury's survey based on what the states themselves declare, and it includes companies in liquidation. There is no official survey of municipal state companies in Brazil — which is why they do not appear here, and why no national total is presented. The two changes of counting criteria — federal in 2019 and state-level in 2020 — appear as separate lines that do not join, following the same rule this site uses for public debt and for unemployment: different rulers are not spliced. None of the counts starts in 1994: SEST only began publishing the count in 2017 and the Treasury in 2019, with 2018 as its base year. Earlier SEST publications counted something else — “companies monitored through the budget” — and splicing them here would create a false series. From 2005 on, the series also includes the count from the Perfil das Empresas Estatais Federais, an annual publication by SEST/DEST that runs from base year 1982 and ends with base year 2015 — it, and not the Boletim das Estatais, is the official source for the FHC, Lula and Dilma period. The Perfil changed criterion midway: up to 2010 it counted the companies whose data appeared in the publication; from 2011 on it counted the universe tracked by DEST, which is larger. That is why the two appear as separate lines rather than spliced together. The directly-controlled line is the only one that crosses both sources with the same meaning — the Union as direct majority shareholder — and for that reason it has been extended back to 2012-2015.

fonte.nome: MGI/SEST — Boletim das Empresas Estatais Federais e Relatório Agregado; Tesouro Nacional — Raio-X das Empresas Estatais Estaduais

notas.nota: In 2019 SEST itself recounted the universe and began including subsidiaries and companies based abroad that already existed and were not being counted. That is why the federal line with subsidiaries is split in two: 146 and 134 under the old criteria, 200 onwards under the new one. The gap between 134 and 200 is not a single company being created.
The Treasury's survey records that the rise from 263 to 302 state-level companies “resulted from a methodological change”. Same solution: two separate lines.

The jump from 122 (2010) to 141 (2012) is not the creation of 19 state companies: it is a change of criterion within the same publication. In 2010 the Perfil counted the companies it published; from 2011 on, the universe tracked by DEST. The 2011 Perfil itself shows both numbers together — 139 and 123 — and that is why the series is split into two lines here. Adding them up or splicing them would produce growth that never happened.

There is no count for 2016, and it is not a collection failure: the Perfil das Estatais ends with base year 2015 and the Boletim das Estatais begins in 2017. The hole in the series is the change of publication. There is also no Perfil edition for base years 2000 to 2003 — the official index jumps from the 1994-1999 volume straight to 2004.

abertura_empresa_db.titulo: How long it takes to open a company in Brazil, by the World Bank's yardstick
abertura_empresa_db.serie_codigo: Doing Business, indicador 'Starting a Business: time (days)', perfil do Brasil
abertura_empresa_db.criterio: the number of calendar days a standard case would take to open a limited liability company, simulated by the World Bank from a fixed script of procedures, with legal advice, in a given city. Up to the 2014 edition only São Paulo was measured; from the 2015 edition on, economies with more than 100 million inhabitants began to be measured by a population-weighted average of two cities — São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. The year shown is that of the report edition, and each edition's data were collected in the previous year.

fonte.nome: Banco Mundial — Doing Business 2020, perfil do Brasil (arquivo oficial)

notas.nota: Doing Business was discontinued by the World Bank in September 2021, after an internal audit found irregularities in the handling of data in the 2018 and 2020 editions. The files remain published, but the World Bank itself stopped endorsing them. This series is here because it is the only measurement with this reach in time, and with that caveat attached to it.
The fall from 107.5 days (2014) to 83.6 (2015) is partly a change of coverage, not only reform: it is the edition in which Rio de Janeiro joins São Paulo in the calculation.

The 2018 and 2019 editions are not in this series: Brazil's profiles for those years publish the São Paulo and Rio figures separately and the population-weighted national average was not found in this collection. The 2004 to 2006, 2011 and 2012 editions were not found either. Because the jump between 2017 and 2020 is large, it stands as a straight stretch between two measured points, not as a known trajectory.

This series and the Mapa de Empresas series measure different things and must not be spliced together. Doing Business counts calendar days of a simulated process with more than a dozen procedures, licensing included; the Mapa de Empresas counts clock hours of two real administrative stages (viability and registration), with no licences and no MEI. Gluing the two together would produce a number that does not exist. They sit side by side here to give the order of magnitude of the change — from about five months to about one day — each with its own yardstick.

It is a nominal change: to see whether there was a real gain, compare it with the PREVIOUS year's inflation — that is what each increase restores.

notas.nota: Series calculated by this site, not published by an official body: it divides one official value by the previous year's.

graficos.titulo: GDP growth — Brazil and the world
graficos.aviso: The bars are Brazil; the line is the world, to give a reference. In the years when the line falls, Brazil's decline has company — 2009 and 2020 were global recessions. Two cautions: the World Bank's world aggregate is weighted by the size of the economies, so it mainly reflects the United States, China and Europe; and the line ends in 2024, the last year measured in that base, while the bars for Brazil run to 2026. Nothing here says that a given year's result is the work of whoever was in the Presidency.
graficos.busca: GDP growth economy recession gross domestic product

graficos.aviso: The two series are on the same axis because both are percentages per year, but they measure different things: the IPCA is the accumulated result of the closed year, the Selic is the target set by the Copom at the end of the year. High interest usually comes after high inflation, not before — the order in time matters when reading it.
graficos.busca: inflation interest rates Selic IPCA prices cost of living

graficos.titulo: Inflation as felt by those who earn least
graficos.aviso: Three measures of the same phenomenon, with different baskets. The IPCA is official inflation, calculated on the consumption of families earning 1 to 40 minimum wages. The INPC uses the same price collection, but weights the basket of families earning 1 to 5 minimum wages — where food, transport and energy take up a larger share of the budget. The third line isolates the Food and beverages group within the IPCA. In the years when the food line shoots above the other two, the same general index meant a tighter squeeze for those who spend proportionally more on food. All three come from IBGE and measure prices, not purchasing power: wages over the same period are not part of this calculation.
sel_inicial: INPC — inflation for families earning 1 to 5 minimum wages

graficos.aviso: Annual average of the selling rate. A higher value means a more devalued real. The exchange rate responds to foreign interest rates, commodity prices and capital flows, as well as to domestic policy — attributing the level to a single administration is a weak reading.
graficos.busca: dollar exchange rate currency real

graficos.titulo: Public debt — three yardsticks, none spliced together
graficos.aviso: Why it does not begin in 1998: the Banco Central's monthly fiscal statistics do not go back beyond December 2001 in any of the public versions. This is not a choice made by this site — the number simply does not exist in that database for earlier years. Within what does exist, there are three distinct measures and they are NOT the same thing at different moments: gross debt under the current methodology (since 2006), gross debt under the pre-2008 criterion (2002-2007) and net debt, which subtracts public sector credits. In December 2006, the month in which two of them overlap, one reads 45.3% and the other 55.5% — same date, different yardsticks. That is why the lines appear separately and are never spliced into a single stroke. All are percentages of GDP: the indicator falls when the economy grows faster than the debt, even if the debt in reais has increased.

balanco.titulo: Como cada governo recebeu e como entregou — dívida bruta, metodologia atual
balanco.nota: Entrada é dezembro do ano anterior à posse; saída é dezembro do último ano completo do mandato. Dilma deixou o cargo em agosto de 2016 e Temer assumiu na mesma data: a série é anual e não separa 2016, então esse ano não é atribuído a nenhum dos dois. Onde a série ainda não existia, está escrito que não há dado — e não zero. A diferença em pontos percentuais descreve o que aconteceu no período, não quem causou.

graficos.busca: debt public debt deficit gross debt net debt

graficos.aviso: The sum of everything the federal government, the states and the municipalities collected in taxes, divided by GDP. It is the measure of the weight of the tax system on the economy, not of the tax a family pays. Two caveats change the reading: the Receita Federal and IBGE calculate the tax burden with different criteria and arrive at different figures for the same year — this series is the Receita's; and there is a break in method from the 2024 report onwards, which stopped including FGTS and contributions to the Sistema S, so that the years up to 2014 and those from 2015 onwards are not strictly comparable. The official series runs to 2024. Below the chart is the dated list of the tax changes of the period, each one with the law or constitutional amendment that established it.
graficos.busca: tax taxes tax burden how much tax is paid

graficos.aviso: The two series are NOT comparable with each other and for that reason appear as separate lines, with no splice. The PME (up to 2015) measured only six metropolitan regions; the PNAD Contínua (since 2012) measures the whole country, using the ILO criterion. Where they overlap, from 2012 to 2015, the difference between the two lines is the difference between the methodologies — not a change in unemployment.
graficos.busca: employment unemployment work jobs PNAD

graficos.titulo: Unemployment, labor underutilisation and discouraged workers
graficos.aviso: The unemployment rate on its own tells part of the story. The composite labor underutilisation rate adds to it those who work fewer hours than they would like and those who are outside the labor force but want and could work — and it is calculated over a larger base, the expanded labor force. That is why it is always higher, without this meaning any contradiction between the two numbers. Discouraged workers are those who would like to work, would be available, and stopped looking because they believed they would not find anything: they do not enter the unemployment rate, because looking for a job is part of the definition of being unemployed. One caveat about comparison: in July 2025 IBGE rebased the entire series on the 2022 Census, which showed a smaller population than the old projections assumed. The rates were recalculated backwards and remain comparable with one another; the absolute numbers in millions of people, before and after the rebasing, are not.

The governor's party is written next to each state because it was requested, and it has to come with the caveat that makes it legible: a state's unemployment rate is NOT a result of the state government. It responds mainly to the local economic structure — the weight of agribusiness, industry, the public sector and informality —, to the national economic cycle and to federal credit, interest-rate and labor policies. States with an export-oriented agricultural economy appear at the top of employment in practically every year, under governors from different parties; states in the North and Northeast appear at the bottom for the same structural reason, also under governors from different parties. Sorting states by this rate and reading the party column as a scoreboard is exactly the error this caveat exists to prevent. The series begins in 2012 because that is when the PNAD Contínua starts covering every unit of the federation; before that, the IBGE survey reached only six metropolitan regions. The controls above allow sorting by value or by state abbreviation, filtering by region and grouping the states into North, Northeast, Central-West, Southeast and South. When grouped, the number next to the region's name is the arithmetic mean of the units in that region — and not the region's rate, which would require weighting each state by the corresponding population. The difference is not small: in the Southeast, São Paulo has more inhabitants than the other three states combined.

graficos.macro: TRABALHO E RENDA · TRANSFERÊNCIA DE RENDA
graficos.titulo: Unemployment and cash transfers, side by side
graficos.aviso: Separate panels, same timeline. This chart makes it possible to look at the two curves together, but it does NOT show that one causes the other. Receiving a cash transfer does not change a person's classification in IBGE's employment survey: someone who receives it and is looking for work is still counted as unemployed; someone who receives it and works is still counted as employed. The two series respond in part to the same causes — recession, pandemic, recovery — and for that reason they move together in several stretches. The unemployment series used here is the PNAD Contínua, which begins in 2012; the earlier period is in the chart of the two surveys.

graficos.macro: TRABALHO E RENDA · TRANSFERÊNCIA DE RENDA
graficos.titulo: Cash transfers — families served and average value
graficos.aviso: The two measures appear in separate panels, one below the other, because they have different units (millions of families and reais per family). Overlaying them in a single chart, with two vertical axes, would make any relationship between them look stronger or weaker depending on the scale chosen. The program changed its name and its rules more than once over the period (Bolsa Família, Auxílio Brasil, Bolsa Família again), and the average amount is in current reais of each year — not adjusted for inflation.

graficos.macro: TRABALHO E RENDA · TRANSFERÊNCIA DE RENDA
graficos.aviso: The BPC is a constitutional right with criteria fixed in law: low-income elderly people and people with disabilities who meet the income test qualify, regardless of any government decision. Its growth reflects above all population aging and wider access, not an annual budget choice.

graficos.titulo: Minimum wage — value since the real
graficos.sub: current R$, value in force at the end of each year, 1994-2026
graficos.aviso: Nominal values: the rise of the line mixes real increases and inflation, and does not, on its own, show more purchasing power. For that, the next chart sets each year's increase beside the INPC. The increase rule changed over the period: until 2006 there was no fixed formula; the appreciation rule — previous year's INPC plus GDP growth from two years before — was agreed in 2007 and set in law from 2011 (Law 12,382/2011, then Law 13,152/2015); not renewed for 2020 to 2022, when increases followed inflation; the formula returned with Law 14,663/2023. Values before the real are not charted, because each is in a different currency that lost value every month: in 1992, Cr$ 96,037.33 in January, Cr$ 230,000.00 in May and Cr$ 522,186.94 in September; in 1993, Cr$ 1,250,700.00 in January, with almost monthly increases after that and the switch to the cruzeiro real in August; in 1994, 64.79 URV from March, which became R$ 64.79 in July.

graficos.aviso: Each increase restores the PREVIOUS year's inflation, not that of its own year: to read a real gain, compare one year's bar with the INPC of the year before. The 1995 change is large because the 1994 value still reflected the URV conversion. The 2026 INPC is partial, because the year is not over.

The IDEB is biennial and begins in 2005. The scale runs from 0 to 10 and combines school pass rates with performance on a standardized assessment.

The gaps are on display on purpose. The measure is self-declared illiteracy — people who say they are unable to read and write a simple note — and it does not capture functional illiteracy.

graficos.aviso: The two series measure different things and for that reason do not form a single curve. Up to 2009 the IBGE published the average number of years of schooling; from 2016 onward it publishes the percentage of adults with twelve or more years of schooling. One is in years, the other in percent: they share the vertical axis for reasons of space, and comparing the height of one with the height of the other means nothing. Between 2010 and 2015 there is neither of the two.

graficos.titulo: Deaths recorded in the Terra Indígena Yanomami
graficos.aviso: This number depends on the capacity to register cases in the field — teams, bases in operation and active case-finding. When that capacity changes, the recorded number changes with it, without real mortality necessarily having changed. Read the series with that caveat, not as a direct measure of mortality.

Rate per 100,000 inhabitants, not an absolute number — it allows years with different populations to be compared. The data come from the SUS death records: changes in the classification of violent deaths of undetermined cause affect the series. Public security is mainly a state responsibility, which limits attributing the number to the federal government.

graficos.aviso: Public security is mainly a state responsibility — the military police, the civil police and the prison system answer to the state government —, which makes this breakdown more pertinent than it would be for an economic indicator. Even so, a state's homicide rate responds to factors that cut across terms of office and borders: trafficking routes, the dynamics among criminal factions, age structure, inequality and the very capacity to register deaths. Changes in the classification of violent deaths of undetermined cause affect comparison between states and between years. The governor's party is next to the state because it was requested; it does not explain the rate, and the order of the list is not a scoreboard between parties. The controls above allow sorting by value or by state abbreviation, filtering by region and grouping the states into North, Northeast, Central-West, Southeast and South. When grouped, the number next to the region's name is the arithmetic mean of the units in that region — and not the region's rate, which would require weighting each state by the corresponding population. The difference is not small: in the Southeast, São Paulo has more inhabitants than the other three states combined.

graficos.macro: TERRA E MEIO AMBIENTE · TERRAS E ASSENTAMENTOS
graficos.aviso: A single chart, with the two stages stacked in different colors. Green is how many families entered land settlement projects; orange is how many land titling documents were delivered — generally to people who were already settled. They are distinct things and are kept apart by color: the total height is not 'families served', because the same family can appear in both colors under different administrations. The default view is by administration because that is how the titling data exists: INCRA publishes totals per term, not year by year. graficos.titulo: STF and the federal Executive branch
graficos.aviso: This block does not classify any decision as anyone's victory or defeat. The same decision is usually both things at once: striking down the cap on precatórios was a relief for those waiting to be paid and a loss of budgetary control for those who manage the budget. What is here is what the court decided, with the date and case number, and the reading is left to whoever reads it. One important convention: each decision appears under the administration that was in office on the DATE OF THE RULING, which is not always the administration that issued the act under challenge — the 2010 decision on the 2000 precatórios amendment is an example.
graficos.busca: supreme court judiciary ruling justice court

graficos.titulo: Public services, red-tape reduction and digitization
graficos.aviso: The list is organized by administration, by the date on which each service or rule took effect — and each item states who authored it, because it is not always the administration of that date. Three cases show why: Pix belongs to the Banco Central, which did not yet have formal autonomy when it was created (Complementary Law 179 came in 2021); the Lei de Acesso à Informação, the Marco Civil and the LGPD spent years in Congress before being signed into law; and gov.br, Meu INSS and the Carteira de Identidade Nacional began under one administration and were expanded under the next. Reading the date as credit for a single administration is, in these cases, an error — which is why the authorship field appears on every line.

graficos.sub: the reader's profile of priorities — it holds the same for every milestone
graficos.aviso_visivel: This is not an assessment of any law. It is the importance you give to each dimension, and it holds the same across every milestone — if legal certainty weighs 20% for you, it weighs 20% in all of them, with no exception by government, sector or rule. Changing a weight changes the emphasis of the reading, never a measured figure, a legal power or a date.
graficos.aviso: The default is one sixth for each dimension, about 16.67% — that is, no declared priority. The further from the centre, the greater the importance you gave that dimension. The dashed line is the default and the solid line is your profile; when you have changed nothing, the two coincide. Six dimensions were chosen because the chart has to fit on a screen and be read at a glance — employment, income, the environment, implementation and distribution have not disappeared: they sit inside the dimension they belong to and appear in each milestone's detail. Legal certainty and freedom of expression have an axis of their own on purpose, so that they are not diluted into an economic category. The profile is saved in this browser, alongside the site's other preferences, and is not sent anywhere.

graficos.titulo: The reach of each milestone, dimension by dimension
graficos.sub: how much the text of each act moves each dimension — and in which direction
graficos.aviso_visivel: The number from 0 to 3 measures the size of the change the text of the act makes, not whether the change was good. Beside each rating comes the direction — expands, restricts, redistributes or disputed — and the article that justifies it. Whether it was good is for you to decide; what is here is what can be checked against the law.
graficos.aviso: Choose a milestone in the dropdown to see its radar; choose two and both appear superimposed, the first as a solid line with round markers and the second dashed with square markers — the difference is not colour alone, so it works in print and for readers who cannot tell the two hues apart. The 'Emphasis by your weights' row uses the profile you built in the previous infographic; if you have not touched it, it is one sixth for each dimension. Each milestone's chevron opens the reasoning behind every rating, with the provision of the law that supports it, and the 'Classification criteria' chevron carries the whole yardstick, which is the same for all 37 milestones.

graficos.sub: 37 laws, constitutional amendments, provisional measures and decrees between 1998 and 2026
graficos.aviso: Each item gives the law with its number and date, what it began to require or allow, whose bill it was and who signed it into law. A bill from the Executive and a bill from Congress are different things, and the difference is written out: several of these laws originated in Parliament and were merely signed by the president of the day. Counting how many laws fell within each one's term measures the legislative calendar, not the agenda of an administration.

graficos.titulo: Federal state-owned companies — two measures that do not add up
graficos.aviso: The two panels measure different universes and can therefore point in opposite directions in the same year. The top one is the aggregate net profit of the federal state-owned companies, measured by the Ministério da Gestão, and it is dominated by Petrobras, Banco do Brasil, BNDES and Caixa. The bottom one is the primary balance measured by the Banco Central, which EXCLUDES Petrobras since 2009 and Eletrobras since 2010 and does not include the public banks — that is, it measures precisely the companies that depend, or may come to depend, on the Tesouro. Adding the two together, or saying that one contradicts the other, is a reading error: they are not talking about the same companies.

graficos.aviso: Net profit or loss of nine companies, one line each. They are in three different orders of magnitude, and that is why the chart does not open with all of them: Petrobras, Banco do Brasil, Caixa and BNDES operate in the tens of billions (Petrobras's profit reached R$ 189 billion); Correios and Infraero, in the billions; Serpro, Embrapa and EBC, in the hundreds of millions. Switched on at the same time, the smaller ones become a straight line pinned to zero. Clicking the names above builds any comparison — the scale adjusts to whatever is selected, and only companies of similar size are worth comparing. Two caveats change the reading. Embrapa and EBC are TREASURY-DEPENDENT state companies: about 98% and 90% of their revenue comes from the Treasury, and the subsidy enters the income statement as revenue — in their case the result reflects budget allocation and provisions, not commercial performance, and Embrapa's loss does not mean inefficiency next to Serpro's profit. And Infraero has a series break in 2023, when it lost 15 airports to concession. The gaps are real: for most of the companies only the recent years could be confirmed, and the chart begins where the source begins, not where the company began. Between 2018 and 2022 the figures for Petrobras, Banco do Brasil, BNDES and Caixa are for the economic group, not the company alone — a change of criterion by the source itself, flagged point by point.

graficos.sub: R$ millions, current values of each year, by company — uneven coverage, see 'How to read'
graficos.aviso_visivel: Each company has its own coverage of years, and that is stated point by point. Banco do Brasil, BNDES and Correios now reach the Lula and Dilma governments; Caixa only starts in 2018, because its financial statements could not be read by this site's collection. The figures are nominal, with no inflation adjustment.

graficos.sub: R$ millions deducted per year, 2016-2024 — a mechanism authorised from 1991 to 2026
graficos.aviso: This bar measures how much was deducted from retirement and survivor benefits as membership dues for associations and unions — not how much was misappropriated. That distinction is the whole point: the CGU established the total deducted and stated that it did not separate, in monetary terms, the authorized share from the unauthorized one. What grounds the suspicion of irregularity is something else: of 1,273 beneficiaries interviewed by the CGU, 1,242 (97.6%) said they had not authorized the deduction, and in a later sample of 952 cases across 29 entities only 28.9% had complete membership documentation. Those are percentages of samples, not of money. Three misreadings circulate and are worth undoing. The first is to call the R$6.3 billion the value of the fraud: that figure is the sum of this same series between 2019 and 2024 — that is, everything deducted in the period. The second is to take the jump in 2023 and 2024 as proof on its own; it is large and it is real, but what happened was growth in the volume deducted, and how much of it was improper is precisely what the investigation is establishing. The third is to read the series as complete: the CGU itself says the figures are underestimated by around 20%, because the INSS database only returns the first ten line items of each benefit. The series starts in 2016 because that is where the CGU extraction starts, and ends in 2024 because the deductions were suspended in April 2025. Added together, the nine bars come to around R$7.9 billion deducted between 2016 and 2024; by April 2026 the INSS had refunded more than R$3 billion to around 4.4 million beneficiaries who filed challenges. The two figures do not subtract from each other: the refunds cover only deductions made between March 2020 and March 2025, and reach those who challenged within the deadline, not the whole of what was deducted.

graficos.sub: R$ millions refunded, cumulative at each date
graficos.aviso: Points at specific dates, not annual averages, and each point already contains the previous ones — this is a cumulative figure. Only the first point has an exact value published by the INSS (R$2,820,799,182.93 on 26/12/2025); the others are rounded figures stated in testimony to the joint congressional inquiry or released to the press. The refunds cover deductions made between March 2020 and March 2025, and the deadline to file a challenge closed on 20 March 2026 — which means the curve tends to flatten because the deadline ran out, not necessarily because the cases did. Refunding is not the same as proving irregularity: the INSS refunded upon the beneficiary's challenge, without case-by-case examination of each deduction.

graficos.sub: R$ at current prices, value in force at the end of each year, 1998-2026
graficos.aviso: This is the other INSS deduction, and it should not be confused with the previous one: here it is what comes out of the salary of someone working, not what used to come out of the benefit of someone already retired. The line shows the ceiling — the limit above which salary generates no contribution and does not count towards the benefit. Nominal values: the rise tracks inflation and minimum-wage adjustments, and does not indicate a real increase in the burden. The rate regime changed three times in the period. Between 1997 and 2007 there were reduced rates for lower salaries, as compensation for the CPMF tax, which is why the table had four brackets for almost all of that time — in 1998 the reduced rates were 7.82% and 8.82%, and became 7.65% and 8.65% when the CPMF rose to 0.38%. With the end of the CPMF, the three rates of 8%, 9% and 11% applied from January 2008 to February 2020. Since 1 March 2020, by effect of Constitutional Amendment 103/2019, the deduction is progressive by bracket (7.5%, 9%, 12% and 14%), as in income tax: the 14% rate applies only to the portion of salary within the top bracket, so that someone earning the ceiling in 2026 has R$988.09 deducted, or 11.66% effective — not 14%, as is commonly read.

graficos.titulo: Ibovespa — what the stock market did each year
graficos.aviso: The government bands say when each year happened, not who produced it. The stock market responds to US interest rates, commodity prices, foreign capital flows and expectations — variables no president controls, and which explain the two extremes of the series: the best year follows the change of exchange-rate regime in 1999, the worst the global financial crisis of 2008. Three reading cautions. The values are NOMINAL: 2002 fell 17% with inflation of 12.5%, and 2004 rose 17.8% with inflation of 7.6% — the second gain is real, the first fall is worse than it looks. The Ibovespa is a total-return index, with dividends reinvested, which makes it yield more than pure price indices such as the S&P 500 in the form they are usually published; placing the two side by side without that correction artificially favors Brazil. And the 2026 bar is partial, measured through September, not a closed year.

graficos.titulo: How many ministries each government had
graficos.sub: posts with ministerial rank on 31 December, 1998-2026
graficos.aviso: The number of ministries measures neither the size of the state nor public spending: it measures how the top tier of government was organized. A portfolio can be created out of policy priority, to accommodate a coalition, or by splitting off from another that continues to exist — and merging two portfolios fires nobody and closes no program. The cost of a ministry lies in the staff and the spending it carries, not in the existence of the minister's post. Two reading traps. The first is comparing numbers from different sources: counting 'ministries' depends on whether or not one adds the Presidency bodies whose heads hold ministerial rank, the Solicitor General's Office, the Comptroller General and the central bank — which is exactly why such different numbers circulate for the same government. This chart states its criterion and applies the same one across all 29 years. The second is reading the steps as annual decisions: the drops in 2015, 2016 and 2019 and the rises in 2003 and 2023 each come from a single provisional measure, issued on day one or mid-term, not from gradual growth. The years 1999 to 2001 are absent because they could not be determined.

graficos.titulo: Federal revenue — how much the federal government collected each year
graficos.aviso: The bars are in December 2025 reais, corrected by IPCA inflation; the dashed line is in the reais of each year, uncorrected. The distance between the two is the inflation of the period, which is why the nominal line looks pinned to the floor in the 1990s: R$ 165 billion in 1998 is the equivalent of R$ 840 billion today. Net of inflation, federal revenue went from R$ 840 billion to R$ 2.76 trillion between 1998 and 2025, real growth of 229% — and it fell, in real terms, in 2009, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2020 and, slightly, in 2012. This chart and the tax-burden chart measure different things and do not contradict each other: revenue can grow a great deal while the burden stays nearly flat, because the burden is revenue divided by GDP, and GDP grows too. These are federal taxes only — state and municipal taxes are not included, and they account for about a third of the total burden. And it is the aggregate of taxes and contributions (the RFB's SUBTOTAL [C]), not the January headline figure, which includes dividends, royalties and concessions and is about R$ 124 billion larger in 2025. Nothing here attributes a year's result to whoever held the presidency.

graficos.titulo: Federal taxes — what each administration changed
graficos.sub: 33 laws, provisional measures and decrees that created, raised, cut or abolished taxes, 1996-2026
graficos.aviso: The height of the bars is a count of acts per term, and the collection is more complete for recent years, with official records digital and searchable, than for the 1990s and 2000s — comparing heights between administrations mostly measures the documentation available. What each bar has that is informative is its composition: red for acts that create or raise a tax, green for those that cut or abolish one, blue for those that change the regime without touching the weight, grey for what is not a tax. The same colours appear on the timeline, on each administration's bar and on each item's tag. Three counting traps that apply to any survey of this kind. A decree that changes 4,000 product codes counts as one act, the same as a law that changes a single rate — which is why “4,000 taxes” and “27 increases” are not numbers of the same kind. Terms have different lengths, and an absolute count favours whoever governed longer. And a tax can go up without anyone signing anything, when a deadline lapses or when the income-tax brackets stay put while wages rise — that kind of increase appears on no list at all. Each item carries the act with its number and date, what it did, and a link to the official text, so the reading does not depend on our classification. An act appears only once, classified by its main effect; Law 15,270/2025, which exempts the bottom and taxes the top, is marked as a cut and explained in the item. The collapsible section below the chart gathers the seven published tallies of the current administration — which range from 24 to 43 — and shows where each difference comes from.
graficos.aviso_visivel: These bars measure how many acts from this collection were made under each term, split by the colour of their effect: red creates or raises a tax, green cuts or abolishes one, blue changes the regime without raising or cutting. The collection documents recent years, with digital and searchable records, far better than the 1990s and 2000s — the current administration's taller bar says, above all, that more documentation about it has been gathered here. The colour composition of each bar says more than its length.

graficos.titulo: Deaths in Brazil — the total and the broad cause groups
graficos.aviso: Start with the total, then tick the groups. 931,895 people died in Brazil in 1998 and 1,532,015 in 2024, an increase of 64%. Before reading that as health getting worse, three figures: the population went from 173.8 million in 2000 to 217.7 million in 2024, and the population aged 60 or over went from 14.8 million to 34.9 million over the same period, growth of 136%. More people die largely because there are more people and because they are older — and dying old is the outcome of a health system that works, not of one that fails. There is a second reason the lines rise that is not epidemiological: deaths with an ill-defined cause fell from 140,929 in 1998 to 69,088 in 2024. Every death that stopped being “ill-defined” went into some other group. Part of the growth in named causes is a better death certificate, not more disease. The twelve groups add up to exactly the total, in every year, and each death counts once, by underlying cause — the disease that began the chain, not the one listed last on the certificate. Covid-19 deaths sit within infectious and parasitic diseases, which is where DATASUS classifies them: that is the 2020 and 2021 jump in that line. The year 2025 is preliminary and should rise. Nothing here attributes a year's result to whoever held the presidency.

graficos.titulo: The diseases that kill the most
graficos.sub: deaths recorded per year, by underlying cause, 1998-2025
graficos.aviso: Fifteen causes chosen from among those most cited in public debate, taken from the list the Ministry of Health uses to tabulate mortality. They do not add up to total deaths and are not meant to: they are slices taken from within the ICD-10 chapters. Under “View” you can switch between disease by disease and six grouped families — cancers, cardiovascular, respiratory, infectious, external causes, and metabolic and neurodegenerative. Each family adds up only the causes on this list, not every cause in the corresponding chapter: “cancers” means the four cancers here, not all neoplasms, which are in the other chart in this section. And a group adds up whatever exists in each year — covid-19 enters from 2020 and dengue has no value for 2025. Tick and untick to compare; the axis adjusts to whatever is selected, so lines of very different magnitudes (Alzheimer's and heart attack, for instance) read better viewed in pairs. Three readings the chart allows that are worth flagging. Covid-19 killed 723,624 people between 2020 and 2025 by underlying cause on the death certificate, 425,218 of them in 2021 alone — more than any other cause on this list in any year. Deaths from Alzheimer's went from 1,076 in 1998 to 30,935 in 2024, forty-five times as many: almost all of that is an ageing population and a diagnosis that now exists, not a new epidemic. And assaults fell from 63,748 in 2017 to 39,946 in 2024, the lowest figure in the series. Dengue is shown by the underlying cause recorded on the certificate, a different and smaller count than epidemiological surveillance: 5,233 here in 2024, about 6,000 in the SINAN tally. The year 2025 is preliminary. Nothing here attributes a year's result to whoever held the presidency.

graficos.titulo: Federal state companies — how many left and how many entered in each presidential term
graficos.aviso_visivel: This chart counts companies that entered and left the official registry — not money raised, nor the size of the company. A single wind farm and Eletrobras each count as one. And leaving the registry does not only mean privatisation: it also covers absorption by another state company, liquidation and transfer — the registry records the date, not the reason.
graficos.aviso: Built by this site from the two registers the SEST publishes: the list of active federal state-owned companies, with each one's creation date, and the list of companies inactive since 1990, with the exit date. There are 239 exits and 41 entries between 1990 and 2023. The series starts in 1990 for two reasons: it is where the inactive register begins, and it is the year the National Denationalization Programme was created, by Law 8,031 of 12 April 1990. Two limits change the reading and have to come before any conclusion. The first: 139 of the 411 companies on the inactive list have no exit date recorded, and 49 of them belong to the Telebrás system — which is why 1998, the year of the largest privatization in Brazil's history, shows only two exits. The 12 holdings auctioned in July that year are in the register with no date. Where the register does not date, the chart does not count. The second: entries are the companies created in that year that still exist today; a company created after 1990 and already wound up does not appear, which understates the older years more than the recent ones — the only entry before 1997 that survived in the register is Conab. Three things have to be said about the first years of the series. First: a good part of the 1990 and 1991 exits is not a sale, it is the administrative reform of Law 8,029 of 12 April 1990, which authorized closing, winding up or merging a set of entities — Embrater, EBTU, Portobras and Embrafilme leave through it, with no auction. Second, and this is the clearest example that leaving the list is not privatizing: Cobal, Cibrazem and CFP leave in 1991 because they were merged with one another, under the same law, to form Conab, which joins the list in their place and started operating on 1 January 1991. Three companies became one; the chart records three exits and one entry, and none of them was sold. Third: the PND auctions do begin on 24 October 1991, with Usiminas, the first federal state company privatized in the country. Between 1991 and 1994 the BNDES counts 33 controlled companies denationalized, with sale revenue of US$ 8.6 billion and US$ 3.3 billion of debt transferred. A warning about how 1992 is attributed. This chart uses the same rule as the rest of the site: a full year goes to whoever held office on 31 December. Since Collor was removed on 2 October 1992, the 14 exits of that year appear under Itamar Franco's term — including auctions held before the removal, such as Companhia Siderúrgica de Tubarão in July and Fosfértil in August. The rule avoids counting 1992 twice, but it does not split the year; anyone who wants the detail has the year-by-year list in the chevron below. Two years account for most of the more recent exits and deserve an explanation. In 1997 there are 26, but almost all of them are the Vale do Rio Doce group going along with the holding: Docegeo, Docenave, Aluvale, Rio Doce Ásia and a dozen more subsidiaries. In 2022 there are 26, and again it is a cascade: Eletrobras takes Furnas, Chesf, Eletronorte, CGT Eletrosul and Eletropar with it in the same move. Counting companies makes a single event look like a sequence. Joining is also almost never a new state company: of the 41 entries, most are subsidiaries or corporate vehicles of Petrobras, Banco do Brasil and Caixa. The chevron below brings the year-by-year list and separates the two things. Nothing here attributes a year's result to whoever held office that year as merit or blame: denationalization processes take years and cross terms.

sel_inicial: Federal — Perfil das Estatais, companies published
Federal — with subsidiaries, criteria up to 2018
graficos.sub: number of companies, by the official counts available, 2005-2025
graficos.aviso: The question “how many state companies does Brazil have” has no single answer, and this chart shows why: there are several different official counts, each correct within its own criterion, and none of them spliced onto the others. The oldest part comes from the “Perfil das Empresas Estatais Federais”, an annual SEST/DEST publication that runs from base year 1982 and ends with base year 2015; the recent part comes from the Boletim das Estatais, which begins in 2017, and the state-level counts from the National Treasury, which begin in 2019 with base year 2018. Between 2015 and 2017 there is a hole, and it is the change of publication, not missing data. The Perfil also changed criterion midway: up to 2010 it counted the companies whose data appeared in the publication, and from 2011 on it counted the universe tracked by DEST, which is larger — the 2011 Perfil itself publishes both numbers side by side, 123 and 139, which is why they appear here as two lines that do not join. Joining any pair of these lines would draw a variation that never happened: it is the same rule this site uses for public debt and unemployment. In 2019 SEST itself recounted the federal universe and began including subsidiaries and companies based abroad that already existed and were not being counted: the total jumps from 134 to more than 200 without a single company having been created. In 2020 the Treasury did the same with state-level companies, from 263 to 302, and records in its report that the rise “resulted from a methodological change”. That is why the directly-controlled line — the Union as direct majority shareholder — is the most reliable of them all: it suffers none of those breaks, means the same thing in the Perfil and in the Boletim, and for that reason has been extended back to 2012 — 46 in 2012, 48 in 2017, 44 in 2025. The line “state companies fell from 209 to 133”, which circulated in 2022, compares the two sides of a recount and measures largely the yardstick, not the State. Municipal state companies are not included: no official survey of them exists in Brazil. That is why this chart presents no national total — adding federal to state-level companies, from different sources and different dates, and calling the result “Brazil's total of state companies” would invent precision the data does not have.
graficos.aviso_visivel: Official counts of companies, not of size or of money. A single wind farm and Eletrobras each count as one. The split lines are changes of counting criteria: where the ruler changes, the line stops and another begins.

fonte.nome: TSE (resultados das eleições de governador de 2010, 2014, 2018 e 2022) e imprensa/Wikipédia para dados de posse, renúncia, cassação e sucessão durante os mandatos, conforme URL registrada em cada mandato individual

notas: Os nomes e partidos de eleição de cada mandato (colunas base) foram coletados de páginas que compilam resultados oficiais do TSE para as eleições de governador de 2010, 2014, 2018 e 2022 (ver 'fonte' de cada item). As trocas de titular durante o mandato (morte, renúncia, cassação, impeachment) e as mudanças de partido foram apuradas uma a uma em reportagens de imprensa, sites oficiais de assembleias legislativas/tribunais e páginas da Wikipédia, com a URL específica registrada em cada item como 'fonte'.

Para os 21 mandatos estaduais não listados aqui com 'houve_troca':true no período 2011-2014 (exceto os 6 confirmados: RJ, PE, AM, SE, MG, TO, RR), não foi feita verificação exaustiva e individualizada de eventuais substituições não amplamente noticiadas; presume-se, com base no padrão observado (poucas trocas, concentradas em governadores que disputaram outros cargos em 2014), que os demais completaram o mandato regularmente, mas isso não foi confirmado positivamente estado a estado.

Para o mandato 2023-2026, o quadro de trocas reflete a onda de renúncias de abril de 2026 (11 governadores, a maioria para concorrer ao Senado, dois — Goiás e Minas Gerais — à Presidência), amplamente noticiada; a data comum de referência (4/4/2026) é o prazo legal de desincompatibilização mencionado nas reportagens consultadas, não necessariamente a data exata de cada renúncia individual, que não foi possível confirmar governador a governador nesta coleta.

O caso do Rio de Janeiro em 2026 (cassação/inelegibilidade de Cláudio Castro e sucessão de Douglas Ruas) ainda não estava definitivamente resolvido nas fontes consultadas em setembro de 2026 (pendência sobre se a sucessão será por eleição direta ou indireta); os dados aqui refletem o quadro conhecido até a data da coleta, não o desfecho final.

'Partido_atual' só é preenchido quando uma mudança de partido do titular eleito (ou do sucessor, nos comentários de 'sucessores') foi encontrada e confirmada em fonte consultada nesta coleta; ausência de 'partido_atual' (valor null) não significa necessariamente que o governador nunca mudou de partido, apenas que nenhuma mudança foi encontrada nas fontes consultadas.

Esta base de dados não contém e não deve ser usada para fazer juízo de valor, comparação entre estados ou partidos, nem qualquer atribuição de causalidade entre o partido do governo estadual e indicadores socioeconômicos como a taxa de desemprego (ver série 'desemprego_uf').

AC.motivo_troca: Gladson Cameli (PP) deixou o cargo até 4/4/2026 para concorrer ao Senado. Mailza Assis (PP), vice-governadora, assumiu; a notícia consultada indica que ela não pretende concorrer nas eleições de outubro de 2026.

AL.motivo_troca: Renan Filho (MDB) renunciou por volta de 2/4/2022 para concorrer ao Senado. Como o vice-governador eleito, Luciano Barbosa, já havia renunciado em 2020 (para assumir a prefeitura de Arapiraca), não havia linha sucessória disponível: a Assembleia Legislativa de Alagoas elegeu indiretamente Paulo Dantas (MDB) para um 'mandato-tampão', que tomou posse em 15/5/2022. Dantas foi afastado do cargo por 180 dias pelo STJ em 11/10/2022 (investigação de suposto esquema de 'rachadinha' na Assembleia); José Wanderley Neto (MDB), seu vice, assumiu interinamente. Dantas venceu a eleição de outubro de 2022 para o mandato seguinte (2023-2026).

sucessores.obs: assumiu após afastamento de Dantas pelo STJ

AL.obs: Não foi possível confirmar nesta coleta quem exerceu o cargo entre a renúncia de Renan Filho (~2/4/2022) e a posse de Paulo Dantas (15/5/2022); provavelmente a presidência da Assembleia Legislativa, mas isso não foi verificado em fonte primária.

AM.motivo_troca: Omar Aziz (PMN) renunciou em 4/4/2014 para concorrer ao Senado. José Melo (PROS), vice-governador, assumiu e completou o mandato; venceu também a eleição de outubro de 2014 para o mandato seguinte.
José Melo (PROS) teve o mandato de 2014 cassado judicialmente; Amazonino Mendes (PDT) assumiu em 2017 após novo pleito e completou o mandato até o fim de 2018.

Wilson Lima (União Brasil) deixou o cargo até 4/4/2026 para concorrer ao Senado. Roberto Cidade (União Brasil), vice-governador, assumiu; segundo a notícia consultada, também não pretende concorrer em outubro de 2026.

CE.motivo_troca: Camilo Santana (PT) renunciou por volta de 1-4/4/2022 para concorrer ao Senado. Izolda Cela (então no PDT, partido do qual se desfiliou em julho de 2022), vice-governadora, completou o mandato, tornando-se a primeira mulher a governar o Ceará.

sucessores.partido: PDT (na posse; deixou o partido em jul/2022)

DF.motivo_troca: Ibaneis Rocha (MDB) deixou o cargo até 4/4/2026 para concorrer ao Senado. Celina Leão (PP), vice-governadora, assumiu.

ES.motivo_troca: Renato Casagrande (PSB) deixou o cargo até 4/4/2026 para concorrer ao Senado. Ricardo Ferraço (MDB), vice-governador, assumiu.

GO.motivo_troca: Marconi Perillo (PSDB) renunciou em 2018 para concorrer nas eleições daquele ano; José Eliton (PSDB), vice-governador, completou o mandato.

Ronaldo Caiado, eleito em 2022 pelo União Brasil e filiado ao PSD por ocasião da renúncia, deixou o cargo até 4/4/2026 para concorrer à Presidência da República. Daniel Vilela (MDB), vice-governador, assumiu.

Carlos Brandão (PSB), vice-governador, completou o mandato e venceu a eleição de outubro de 2022 para o mandato seguinte.
